titles.l2: Two strange lengths, one ordinary answer

kernelIdea: The irrationals are not closed under addition or multiplication and contain neither 0 nor 1 — they are not a field. But if a is irrational so are −a and 1/a, and a nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational.

kernels.l1: Two strange numbers can add up to a perfectly ordinary one.
kernels.l2: Two numbers that are not fractions can add up to a number that is. So the not-fractions do not behave like a tidy number system.
kernels.l3: Adding or multiplying two irrational numbers can land you back among the fractions, so the irrationals are not a tidy system. But the opposite of an irrational is irrational, and so is a fraction times an irrational.
kernels.l4: The irrationals are not closed under addition or multiplication and contain neither 0 nor 1, so they are not a field. But −a and 1/a are irrational whenever a is, and a nonzero rational times an irrational is irrational.
kernels.l5: The irrationals fail closure but are stable under negation, reciprocal, and multiplication by nonzero rationals; each proof is a suppose not using closure of ℚ.
kernels.l6: The irrationals are a set, not a field; their stability properties all follow by contradiction from closure of ℚ.
kernels.l7: The irrationals fail closure under addition and multiplication and contain no additive or multiplicative identity, so they form no field; stability under negation, inversion, and scaling by nonzero rationals is proved by contradiction from closure of ℚ.
kernels.l8: The irrationals are the complement of a subfield and hence not a subfield; that irrational^irrational can be rational is a famous nonconstructive existence proof.
